nameStory: The Fourteen-spotted Lady Beetle gets its name from the distinctive pattern of black spots on its wing covers - count them carefully and you'll find exactly fourteen! Like other lady beetles, it was named after the Virgin Mary ("Our Lady") in medieval Europe, where these helpful garden insects were considered a blessing from above.
description: This small, dome-shaped beetle is one of the classic lady beetles you'll spot crawling on plants throughout New England. Its bright yellow to orange wing covers are decorated with fourteen black spots arranged in a specific pattern that makes it easy to identify once you know what to look for. Like all lady beetles, it has a smooth, glossy shell and tiny legs that tuck neatly underneath its rounded body when threatened.

idTips.label: Fourteen black spots
idTips.description: Count the distinct black spots on the wing covers - there should be exactly fourteen, though they may vary slightly in size and some might appear to merge together

idTips.label: Yellow-orange coloration
idTips.description: Wing covers range from bright yellow to warm orange, with a smooth, glossy finish that feels hard and polished to the touch

idTips.label: Small dome shape
idTips.description: Body is perfectly dome-shaped when viewed from the side, about the size of a small pea, and feels smooth and firm when gently handled

idTips.label: Black head and pronotum
idTips.description: The head and the shield-like section behind it are typically black, creating a nice contrast with the spotted wing covers

idTips.label: Clubbed antennae
idTips.description: Short antennae that end in small clubs, often tucked close to the head and barely visible unless you look closely

habitat: Look for Fourteen-spotted Lady Beetles in gardens, fields, forest edges, and anywhere aphids congregate - including on roses, vegetables, and wild plants like goldenrod. They're particularly common in sunny, open areas with diverse plant life, from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England. You'll often find them on the undersides of leaves where their prey hides.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active on warm days, often seen sunning themselves on south-facing surfaces before moving to plants to hunt aphids.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible hunting on plants, mating, and laying eggs. Look for both adults and their spiky, alligator-like larvae on aphid-infested plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults feed heavily to build up fat reserves for winter, often gathering in large groups on warm surfaces. They begin seeking overwintering sites under rocks, logs, and leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Hidden away in protected spots like under bark, stones, or fallen logs in a dormant state. Occasionally visible on unusually warm winter days.

funFact: A single Fourteen-spotted Lady Beetle can devour over 5,000 aphids in its lifetime, making it one of nature's most efficient pest control agents - so effective that they're actually raised commercially and sold to gardeners as living insecticides!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other spotted lady beetles, but the key is counting those spots - other species have different numbers (seven, nine, fifteen, etc.). Remember "Fourteen is the feature" - no other common New England lady beetle has exactly this spot count.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bugs," lady beetles are actually beetles (not true bugs), and the term "ladybug" versus "lady beetle" often sparks friendly debates among naturalists. The "P-14" nickname comes from scientific shorthand, where "P" represents the genus Propylea and "14" refers to the fourteen spots.
compareHints: As the only Propylea species in New England, compare it with other spotted lady beetles like the Nine-spotted or Seven-spotted Lady Beetles. The Fourteen-spotted is distinguished by its specific spot count and typically more yellow coloration, while most other common lady beetles tend toward red or have fewer, larger spots.
